Q: Exceptions - String to Integer A:

Even though your program produced the correct output, it was still marked wrong because it caught a general Exception. The problem specifically requires the use of string-to-integer conversion with proper exception handling, and in Python, a failed int() conversion raises a ValueError. Catching the specific exception shows correct understanding of exception handling, which is what the compiler checks for. Using a broad Exception technically works, but it doesn’t meet the problem’s strict requirements.
You can try this:

if __name__ == '__main__':
    S = input()
    try:
        print(int(S))
    except ValueError:
        print("Bad String")

Q: Github Actions self hosted runner on macOS tries to checkout repository forever A:

The macOS Keychain API serializes access requests. When multiple actions/checkout jobs attempt to store credentials simultaneously via git-credential-osxkeychain, they compete for the keychain lock. macOS 15.2 (Tahoe) may have tightened security policies around keychain access, triggering this behavior where it previously worked.

Solution 1: Disable Credential Persistence (Recommended)

If your workflows only need to clone/checkout and don't perform subsequent git operations requiring authentication:

yaml

- uses: actions/checkout@v6
  with:
    persist-credentials: false

This bypasses git-credential-osxkeychain entirely by not storing credentials after checkout.

Limitations: Won't work if your workflow needs to push commits or access private submodules in later steps.

Solution 2: Configure Git Credential Helper Globally

On your self-hosted runner, disable osxkeychain in favor of in-memory or file-based storage:

bash

# Disable osxkeychain entirely
git config --system credential.helper ""

# Or use cache (stores in memory for 15 minutes)
git config --system credential.helper cache

This affects all git operations on the runner. The --system flag ensures it applies to the runner's user account.

Solution 3: Pre-unlock Keychain

If you must use osxkeychain, unlock the keychain before jobs start. Add this to your runner's startup script or use a pre-job hook:

bash

security unlock-keychain -p "${RUNNER_KEYCHAIN_PASSWORD}" \
  ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db

# Set timeout to prevent re-locking during jobs
security set-keychain-settings -t 3600 ~/Library/Keychains/login.keychain-db

Security consideration: This keeps the keychain unlocked, which may not be acceptable in all environments.

Debugging

To confirm keychain contention is the issue:

bash

# Watch for credential helper processes
ps aux | grep git-credential

# Monitor keychain operations
sudo log stream --predicate 'process == "git-credential-osxkeychain"' --level debug

If you see multiple git-credential-osxkeychain processes stuck in D (uninterruptible sleep) state, this confirms the keychain serialization issue.

References

  • GitHub Actions Checkout v6 documentation - see persist-credentials option

  • Git Credentials Documentation - explains credential helper configuration

  • macOS Security Command Manual - security command reference

Q: Using advisory locks to coordinate database activity A:

When I try very similar code to yours:

with Session(self.engine) as session:
    result = session.execute(
        select(func.pg_try_advisory_lock(123))
    )    
    success = next(result)[0]
    if not success:
        print('Could not acquire 123 lock.  Exiting.')
        sys.exit(1)
             
    print('Acquired 123 lock.')
    print('Calling session.commit()')
    session.commit()
    input('Press Enter to release lock.')

When I run this code twice from separate terminals, I get the "Acquired 123 lock" message in both terminals, without pressing Enter in either one.

If I take out the commit call, I do get the "Could not acquire 123 lock" message as expected from the second invocation.

I am creating the engine a bit differently than in your example:

engine = create_engine(
    engine_string,
    isolation_level='REPEATABLE READ',
    poolclass=sqlalchemy.pool.NullPool
)

Could this explain the difference?

Q: Difference between hdpi and large-hdpi? A:

From the API documentation:

http://developer.android.com/guide/practices/screens_support.html

... two devices that both report a screen size of normal might have actual screen sizes and aspect ratios that are slightly different when measured by hand. Similarly, two devices that report a screen density of hdpi might have real pixel densities that are slightly different. Android makes these differences abstract to applications, so you can provide UI designed for the generalized sizes and densities and let the system handle any final adjustments as necessary.

Also note (same link):

Beginning with Android 3.2 (API level 13), these size groups are deprecated in favor of a new technique for managing screen sizes based on the available screen width

This is where "smallestWidth sw600dp" and friends come in:

http://developer.android.com/guide/practices/screens_support.html#DeclaringTabletLayouts

The main issue is "How can the Android API accommodate the wide range of devices with the minimum effort on the part of the developer?"
